1.pericope_label: The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying, Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words. Then I went down to the potter’s house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels. And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it. Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying, O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take three chapters together as one compilation of two symbolical actions; Ellicott places the potter's field, describes the two wheels, and locates the marring in the material rather than the workman.

Gill and Calvin reach independently for the same argument from the less to the greater, that the potter did not make the clay he shapes whereas God made the men he deals with; Gill also weighs and rejects a site for the potter's house beneath the temple.

Clarke describes the wheel and the accident that spoils a vessel, and turns the verse into a protest against any decree that makes souls for perdition; Wesley grants the absolute power and bounds it by justice.
Henry reads the errand rather than the doctrine: the prophet was sent not to preach a sermon but to receive one ready prepared.

debates.question: How much of the book does this prophecy belong to?

positions.position: A distinct prophecy, connectable with what precedes since it takes up the destruction threatened there.
Three chapters together as one compilation of two symbolical actions with their interpretation.
A last warning whose rejection brings the same symbol back more decisively later.
Low-lying and outside the city near the potter's field; not beneath the temple, as some suppose.
The potter's field itself, on the southern face of the valley, where the soil is still such clay.

debates.question: How did the potter's wheel work?

positions.position: A moving stone turning on a fixed one below and carrying the surface where the vessel was made.
Two wheels: a horizontal one driven by the feet and a smaller one turning under the hands.
It did not stand in the working, or gravel worked into the mass made a breach.
It was spoiled while still soft in the potter's hand.
Through a defect in the material, and in application through the resistance of the human agents God is fashioning.

debates.question: What does the potter's right over the clay amount to?

positions.position: More than the potter's, since the potter did not make his clay and God made the men he deals with.
Absolute, but exercised as a just judge rendering to every man according to his works.
Neither fatalism crushing freedom nor a sovereignty dissolved into human choice: the clay may resist or yield.
A right to reject and remake, but not to make souls on purpose for perdition.

outliers.claim: Reads the sending as a lesson in itself: the prophet was sent not to preach a sermon but to receive one ready prepared, and those who would know God's mind must attend where his words are heard.
Raises a difficulty against his own identification of the site: buying the field to bury strangers implies waste ground whose use had been exhausted.

themes: The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying,
Arise, and go down to the potter’s house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words.
Then I went down to the potter’s house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.
And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying,
O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.

7.pericope_label: At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it; if that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them. And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, to build and to plant it; if it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good. Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, saying, Return ye now every one from his evil way. And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both catch the potter's verb behind the framing of evil, and both read the people's answer as present and repeated rather than past; Ellicott adds that the vessel's form is not unalterably fixed.

Gill extends the rule by name to Jews and Gentiles; Calvin fills out both halves of it, marks the level at which the figure is pitched, and reads the refusal as the obstinacy of men trusting Assyria and Egypt by turns.
Clarke states the rule as the decree by which the whole of God's conduct towards man is regulated, so that sentence and promise alike turn on what the man does next.
Henry works the potter's image out and has the ruin already in progress, with the invitation offered so they may meet God in the way of his judgments and prevent his further proceedings.

debates.question: What kind of rule is stated in these verses?

positions.position: The decree by which the whole of God's conduct towards man is regulated.
The same rule, extended by name to Jews and Gentiles alike.
The popular statement of the figure, pitched lower than the apostle's use of it because it turns on repentance.

debates.question: Is the threatened ruin already in operation or still contingent?

positions.position: In progress: providence in all its operations is plainly working that way.
Contingent: the vessel's form is not unalterable, and the shape is shown to frighten them into taking the warning.
Suspended: vengeance hangs over their heads unless they turn in time.

debates.question: Is There is no hope despair or defiance?

positions.position: Defiance, and in the present tense: they say, not they said, of an action repeating itself.
Not a denial of mercy but the prophet's own despair of reclaiming them.
A weary it is all over, bound up with trusting now the Assyrians and now the Egyptians.

debates.question: What is the force of the word rendered frame?

positions.position: The potter's own verb, from which the Hebrew word for potter derives; the design in view is an evil plot.
Worked out as an image: God frames evil as the potter frames a vessel, so as to answer the end.

outliers.claim: Presses the promising half of the rule further than the others: God does not merely pardon but is ready to load with every blessing those he had rejected as enemies, and will equally tread in the dust the people he has favoured if the favours are abused.
Holds that the shape of the vessel now in hand is shown in terrorem, its form not unalterably fixed, so that the threat is an invitation to repentance rather than a sentence.

themes: At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it;
If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them.
And at what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to build and to plant it;
If it do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, then I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit them.

Now therefore go to, speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the Lord; Behold, I frame evil against you, and devise a device against you: return ye now every one from his evil way, and make your ways and your doings good.
And they said, There is no hope: but we will walk after our own devices, and we will every one do the imagination of his evil heart.

13.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Ask ye now among the heathen, who hath heard such things: the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing. Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken? Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing. I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy; I will shew them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.

schools.summary: Ellicott removes the interpolated words that make a man the subject of the snow question, supplies the prophets and teachers as the unnamed cause of the stumbling, and denies that the hissing and head-shaking mean contempt; Keil and Delitzsch take the vanity for the idols themselves.

Gill describes the snows of Lebanon and the traveller who would not pass such water untasted; Calvin turns to the Gentiles as witnesses, illustrates the folly from the river at his own door, and catches the wordplay between the ancient paths and the perpetual hissing.

Clarke reports a variant reading of the virgin's name, makes the hissing contempt, and quotes an English proverb on the east wind; Wesley reduces the parable to a maxim and names the patriarchs who walked the ancient paths.

debates.question: Who or what is the subject of the question about the snow of Lebanon?

positions.position: A man, and the folly is his: he would not pass such water untasted, or trade a watered farm for a barren rock, or forsake a greater good for a less.
Not a man at all: the words are interpolated, and the question is whether the snow fails from the rock and the streams from afar dry up.

debates.question: What does the passer-by's reaction express?

positions.position: Contempt: a shrieking and hissing.
Horror and pity rather than scorn: a sound-word for a shudder, and a head-shake of bemoaning.
A wordplay: the perpetual of the hissing answers the ancient of the paths, one looking backward and the other forward.

debates.question: Who caused the stumbling, and what is the vanity?

positions.position: The prophets and teachers who misled the people; and the word is not the usual one for vanity but the one used elsewhere of idols.
The idols themselves, to which sacrifices were kindled.
Forsaking the worship of God and following idols.
What was left is named by its walkers: the way of Noah and Abraham and Jacob.

debates.question: How is the east wind to be read?

positions.position: By its character: it parches and blasts grain and trees, and men and cattle suffer.
As the fiercest wind of that country, scattering them as it scatters chaff.
Manuscripts vary between with and as an east wind, without much affecting the sense.
A comparison is intended whichever particle is read.

outliers.claim: Quotes the old English metrical proverb that when the wind blows from the east it is good for neither man nor beast.
Illustrates the folly from his own doorstep: if a man today would not drink the river flowing past him but set off to taste the spring, everyone would laugh at the madness.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Ask ye now among the heathen, who hath heard such things: the virgin of Israel hath done a very horrible thing.
Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon which cometh from the rock of the field? or shall the cold flowing waters that come from another place be forsaken?
Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;
To make their land desolate, and a perpetual hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, and wag his head.
I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy; I will shew them the back, and not the face, in the day of their calamity.

18.pericope_label: Then said they, Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words. Give heed to me, O Lord, and hearken to the voice of them that contend with me. Shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them. Yet, Lord, thou knowest all their counsel against me to slay me: forgive not their iniquity.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the prayer as the exact answer to the resolve not to give heed, recovers the vividness of the pit, and declines to judge the imprecation; Keil and Delitzsch treat the last verse as the summing up of the whole prayer and prefer the written text to the margin.

Gill holds that God attends to his ministers when men will not, and that no counsel is laid too deep for him; Calvin makes the turn to God a device of vehemence and weighs impiety against inhumanity before defending the curses as dictated by the Spirit.

Clarke reads smiting with the tongue as a judicial punishment and denies that the execrations are prayers at all; Wesley puts the plotters' boast in their own mouths and answers the question of imprecation flatly against the practice.
Henry generalises the plot into the standing method of persecutors, who do in concert what they cannot do apart.

debates.question: What did the plotters rely on?

positions.position: That they had guidance enough in the Law, the priests and agreeable prophets, and that it would continue whatever the threats.
That they had the church on their side, the priests and prophets knowing God's mind as well as he.
Nothing peculiar to them: it is the standing method of persecutors to do in concert what they cannot do apart.

debates.question: What is smiting him with the tongue?

positions.position: Slander: stopping his mouth and representing him as the thing the people hate.
A punishment on the tongue, as false testimony is punished in eastern countries with a leather strap or a bodkin.

debates.question: What does standing before God mean here?

positions.position: Intercession: he was their continual intercessor.
The act of worship and communion with God, in its commoner sense.
Not prayers at all, but prophetic declarations of judgments about to be poured out.
Not lawful for Christians, whose duty is to pray for their enemies' conversion.
Wrong in itself, since God's children are to bear all injuries, but he was moved by the Holy Spirit, and what the Spirit dictates is not condemned.
Undecidable, and not ours to judge another man's servant; righteous anger is at least a step towards righteous love.

debates.question: How should the closing verse be read?

positions.position: As the summing up of the whole prayer, with the written text preferred to the marginal reading.
Without the supplied word thus, which weakens rather than emphasises the prayer.
As resting on the plain point that God knows men's counsels however deep they are laid.

outliers.claim: Recovers a vividness familiarity has worn away from the digged pit: the man was being treated as a beast, the prophet who sought their good hunted like the wolf they trapped and killed.

Weighs the two sins against each other: impiety is the more detestable, since God is above all mortals, but inhumanity has more baseness, being grosser and more evident, and men who hide their perfidy show it as soon as they deal with men.

themes: Then said they, Come, and let us devise devices against Jeremiah; for the law shall not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise, nor the word from the prophet. Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words.
Give heed to me, O Lord, and hearken to the voice of them that contend with me.
Shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember that I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them.

Therefore deliver up their children to the famine, and pour out their blood by the force of the sword; and let their wives be bereaved of their children, and be widows; and let their men be put to death; let their young men be slain by the sword in battle.
Let a cry be heard from their houses, when thou shalt bring a troop suddenly upon them: for they have digged a pit to take me, and hid snares for my feet.

Yet, Lord, thou knowest all their counsel against me to slay me: forgive not their iniquity, neither blot out their sin from thy sight, but let them be overthrown before thee; deal thus with them in the time of thine anger.
